## Medical vs. Research Accelerators — What Changes for AI

| | Research machine | Clinical machine |
|---|---|---|
| **Downtime tolerance** | Hours–days acceptable | Patient appointments cannot be cancelled |
| **Fault data** | Abundant — machine is pushed to limits | Scarce by design — engineered to be safe |
| **Real-time budget** | Seconds to minutes | ms to μs for pulse-to-pulse corrections |
| **Regulatory overhead** | Internal safety rules | IEC 62304, ISO 13485, FDA/CE for software |

::: {.warning-box style="margin-top: 0.8em;"}
**The key inversion:** clinical machines are engineered to *avoid* faults — so fault data is scarce by design.
This is the opposite of the "big data" assumption most ML workflows make.
:::

::: notes
This table is the most important slide in the first block. Everything else flows from it.

The "scarce fault data" row shapes every design choice: why we use autoencoders (unsupervised, no fault labels), why we use Bayesian optimisation (sample-efficient), why we use physics-informed models (can work with little data).

The regulatory row: IEC 62304 is the software lifecycle standard for medical device software. Any AI in a clinical control loop is in scope. This requires audit trails and explainability — not as extras, but as compliance requirements.
:::

# The Physics–AI Connection {.section-divider background-color="#0a1520"}

::: {style="color: #22d3ee; font-size: 1.3em; font-weight: 600; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
Where modern machine learning came from
:::

::: notes
Before diving into the use cases, I want to take 8 minutes to give you the historical and conceptual context. This is not a detour — it's the foundation.
:::

---

## Physics Built AI — Then Forgot

::: {.col-left}

**1943** — McCulloch & Pitts: mathematical neurons from neuroscience

**1958** — Rosenblatt: perceptron (early AI optimism, then first winter)

**1982** — **John Hopfield** (physicist, Princeton): applies *spin-glass physics* to associative memory.
The neural network *energy function* = a Lyapunov function from statistical mechanics.

**1983–1985** — **Boltzmann machines** (Hinton & Sejnowski): sampling from the Boltzmann distribution directly imports the canonical ensemble from thermodynamics.

**1986** — Backpropagation made practical: Rumelhart, Hinton, Williams.

:::

::: {.col-right}

::: {.highlight-box}
**The Hopfield insight (1982)**

An Ising-like spin system:

$$E = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{ij} w_{ij} s_i s_j$$

converges to stored *memories* (attractors).

The same math describes how associative recall works in a neural network.

This is spin-glass physics applied to computation.
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
Hopfield's 1982 paper in PNAS is one of the most cited papers in physics and neuroscience combined. He was a condensed matter physicist who saw the parallel between spin systems and associative memory. The energy function is a Lyapunov function — it guarantees convergence to attractors (stored patterns).

The Boltzmann machine learning rule is literally the Gibbs sampling algorithm for the Boltzmann distribution. The partition function, the free energy — these are all directly from statistical mechanics.

Physics gave ML its mathematical foundations. The community then moved to computer science departments and largely forgot the origin.
:::

---

## The Nobel Prize in Physics 2024

::: {style="text-align: center; margin-top: 0.8em;"}
::: {style="font-size: 1.1em; color: #22d3ee; font-weight: 600;"}
*"for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks"*
:::

**John J. Hopfield** and **Geoffrey E. Hinton** — Nobel Prize in Physics 2024
:::

::: {.col-left style="margin-top: 1em;"}
**Why it matters for this lecture:**

- The Nobel Committee awarded it in **Physics** (not Computer Science or AI)
- This is a formal recognition: the mathematical foundations of neural networks are physics
- Hopfield networks, Boltzmann machines → today's transformers, diffusion models
- The tools we will use today (PyTorch, automatic differentiation) trace directly to this lineage
:::

::: {.col-right style="margin-top: 1em;"}
::: {.highlight-box}
**Physics–ML connections still active today**

- Renormalisation group ↔ hierarchical feature learning (Mehta & Schwab, 2014)
- Statistical mechanics of learning ↔ generalisation bounds
- Path integrals ↔ variational inference and diffusion models
- Energy-based models ↔ Boltzmann machines, score matching

Accelerator physicists are natural ML practitioners.
:::
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
The Nobel Prize was awarded in October 2024, just before this lecture. I think it's the right place to start: it legitimises the connection between physics and ML for physicists who might have thought "ML is for computer scientists."

The renormalisation group connection is genuinely deep: the RG coarse-graining procedure (integrating out high-frequency modes) is structurally similar to how deep networks progressively abstract away fine-grained features. Mehta & Schwab made this precise in 2014.

Energy-based models are currently one of the most active research areas in deep learning. Yann LeCun (Turing Award) has been pushing this direction for a decade.

For us as accelerator physicists: we already think in terms of Hamiltonians, phase spaces, and energy functions. ML is a natural extension of our toolkit.
:::

## AI Arrives at Accelerators — A Timeline

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

| Year | Milestone |
|------|-----------|
| **1993** | First neural networks for accelerator control — ALS, SLAC |
| **2016** | Reinforcement learning for CERN injection optimisation (pilot) |
| **2019** | Bayesian optimisation at LCLS (Duris et al., *PRL* 124, 2020) — 4× faster tuning |
| **2020** | Autoencoder fault detection in SRF cavities — JLab (Tennant et al., *PRAB* 23, 2020) |
| **2021** | Cheetah: PyTorch-differentiable beam simulator (Kaiser et al., *PRAB* 27, 2024) |
| **2022** | RL-based longitudinal control at CERN SPS |
| **2024** | ARTIFACT/KARA: **−30% beam losses** with online RL surrogate |
| **2025** | TwinRISE (Horizon Europe): federated digital twins, 19 institutions |
| **2026** | → Foundation models for accelerators (pre-training on multi-facility data) |

:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.5em;"}
30 years from first experiments to production deployment. The exponential part is now.
:::

::: notes
LCLS (Linac Coherent Light Source at SLAC) used BO to tune 9 quadrupole magnets in the beam transport. Compared to expert operators, BO found equally good or better settings 4× faster.

JLab used an autoencoder trained only on normal SRF cavity waveforms. Any cavity trip outside the training distribution → high reconstruction error → flagged anomaly. This is exactly use case 1 in this lecture.

The ARTIFACT/KARA result is my own group's work: online reinforcement learning with a Cheetah-based surrogate reduced beam losses by 30% at the KARA storage ring at KIT.

The "foundation model" entry for 2026 is aspirational but realistic. AlphaFold-style pre-training on pooled accelerator data from multiple facilities could give any new facility a strong starting model.
:::

# Use Case 1 {.section-divider background-color="#0a1520"}

::: {style="color: #22d3ee; font-size: 1.6em; font-weight: 800; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
RF Fault Detection
:::

Autoencoders on cavity IQ waveforms

---

## The RF Fault Detection Problem

**Every RF pulse generates a waveform.**

On a superconducting cavity, we record the **IQ signals** (in-phase + quadrature) — one pair per cavity per pulse at ~1 kHz.

A fault shows up in the waveform:

- **Quench** — sudden amplitude drop during flat-top
- **Detuning** — cavity goes off-resonance; Q component becomes non-zero
- **Multipacting** — oscillations superimposed on the flat-top

::: {.highlight-box style="margin-top: 0.8em;"}
**The challenge:** clinical machines are designed to be safe → faults are rare → very few labelled fault examples.

**The solution:** train on *normal pulses only*.
Faults = high reconstruction error. No fault labels needed.
:::

::: notes
IQ signals: the RF signal at cavity resonance is demodulated into in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q) components. On a well-tuned on-resonance cavity, I is trapezoidal and Q is near zero. Any off-resonance operation or fault appears in the Q signal.

This is deployed in production at JLab (CEBAF), SNS at Oak Ridge, and in our research at GANIL/SPIRAL2.
:::

---

## What the Data Looks Like

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-align: center

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

def _envelope(t, rise=0.10, fall=0.85):
    return np.piecewise(t.astype(float),
        [t < rise, (t >= rise) & (t <= fall), t > fall],
        [lambda t: t / rise, 1.0, lambda t: (1.0 - t) / (1.0 - fall)])

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 256)
noise = 0.025

def normal(seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    env = _envelope(t)
    return env + rng.normal(0, noise, 256), rng.normal(0, noise, 256)

def quench(seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    I, Q = normal(seed)
    qp = rng.integers(80, 160)
    I[qp:] = rng.normal(0, noise/2, 256-qp)
    Q[qp:] = rng.normal(0, noise/2, 256-qp)
    return I, Q

def detuning(seed=2):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    env = _envelope(t)
    freq = rng.uniform(3, 7)
    I = env * np.cos(2*np.pi*freq*t) + rng.normal(0, noise, 256)
    Q = env * np.sin(2*np.pi*freq*t) + rng.normal(0, noise, 256)
    return I, Q

def multipacting(seed=3):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    I, Q = normal(seed)
    s, e = 40, 210
    freq = rng.uniform(6, 12)
    amp = rng.uniform(0.12, 0.22)
    tt = np.linspace(0, 1, e-s)
    I[s:e] += amp * np.sin(2*np.pi*freq*tt)
    Q[s:e] += amp * np.cos(2*np.pi*freq*tt)
    return I, Q

cases = [("Normal", normal, "#22d3ee"), ("Quench", quench, "#f87171"),
         ("Detuning", detuning, "#fb923c"), ("Multipacting", multipacting, "#a78bfa")]

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=4,
    subplot_titles=[f"{n} — I" for n,_,_ in cases] + [f"{n} — Q" for n,_,_ in cases],
    vertical_spacing=0.12, horizontal_spacing=0.06)

for col, (name, fn, color) in enumerate(cases, 1):
    I, Q = fn()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=I, line=dict(color=color, width=1.5),
                             name=name, showlegend=(col==1)), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=Q, line=dict(color=color, width=1.5),
                             showlegend=False), row=2, col=col)

fig.update_layout(
    height=420, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=11),
    margin=dict(l=30, r=10, t=50, b=10),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.12, x=0.5, xanchor="center",
                font=dict(color="#e2e8f0")),
)
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=False, zeroline=False, color="#475569")
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048", zeroline=False, color="#475569")
fig.show()
```

::: notes
Row 1 = I component (in-phase), Row 2 = Q component (quadrature).

Normal: I is a clean trapezoid, Q is near zero. Detuning: strong Q signal — the cavity went off-resonance. Quench: sharp drop in both I and Q mid flat-top. Multipacting: high-frequency oscillations superimposed.

In the companion notebook, participants generate this dataset and explore it interactively.
:::

---

## The Autoencoder Model

```{python}
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class RFAutoencoder(nn.Module):
    """1-D conv autoencoder for IQ waveform anomaly detection."""

    def __init__(self, seq_len=256, latent_dim=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv1d(2, 32, kernel_size=8, stride=4, padding=2),  # (2, 256) → (32, 64)
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Conv1d(32, 64, kernel_size=4, stride=2, padding=1), # → (64, 32)
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Flatten(),
            nn.Linear(64 * 32, latent_dim),                        # → latent vector
        )
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(latent_dim, 64 * 32),
            nn.Unflatten(1, (64, 32)),
            nn.ConvTranspose1d(64, 32, kernel_size=4, stride=2, padding=1),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.ConvTranspose1d(32, 2, kernel_size=8, stride=4, padding=2),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.decoder(self.encoder(x))
```

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.5em;"}
Input: `(batch, 2, 256)` — 2 channels (I + Q), 256 time points.
Anomaly score = mean squared reconstruction error per pulse.
:::

::: notes
Two design choices to highlight:
1. Input encodes both I and Q simultaneously as two channels — the model learns the joint distribution.
2. Latent dimension 16 is small — the bottleneck forces compression to the "normal pulse manifold."

At inference: compute reconstruction error for every pulse. Normal → low error. Faults → high error (model never saw them during training).
:::

---

## Training and Detection Result

```{python}
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset

model = RFAutoencoder(seq_len=256, latent_dim=16)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

# Train on normal pulses ONLY — no fault labels required
X_normal = X_train[y_train == 0]
loader   = DataLoader(TensorDataset(X_normal), batch_size=64, shuffle=True)

for epoch in range(40):
    for (batch,) in loader:
        loss = ((batch - model(batch)) ** 2).mean()
        optimizer.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optimizer.step()

# Score every pulse (normal + faults)
with torch.no_grad():
    scores = ((X_test - model(X_test)) ** 2).mean(dim=(1, 2))

threshold   = scores[y_test == 0].quantile(0.95)
predictions = (scores > threshold).long()
```

::: {.col-left}
::: {.metric}
**ROC-AUC > 0.99**
on held-out test set
:::
:::

::: {.col-right}
::: {.qr-box}
**Notebook 01** — run this yourself
`notebooks/01_fault_detection/`
:::
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
Key points:
- Training uses only ~800 normal pulses. No fault data needed.
- Threshold at 95th percentile of normal scores → ~5% false-positive rate on normal data.
- In production, the threshold is tuned based on cost of false positives (unnecessary beam stops) vs false negatives (missed faults).
- ROC-AUC > 0.99 means the anomaly score almost perfectly separates normal from fault pulses.

# Use Case 2 {.section-divider background-color="#0a1520"}

::: {style="color: #22d3ee; font-size: 1.6em; font-weight: 800; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
Beam Tuning with Bayesian Optimisation
:::

Cheetah · differentiable accelerator simulation

---

## The Daily Startup Problem

**Every morning on a clinical machine:**

1. Run QA checks (output, flatness, energy)
2. Tune steering magnets and quadrupoles until beam quality is within spec
3. Hand off to clinical staff

Currently: **20–45 min of physicist time**, largely manual — $n$ correctors × $k$ quads = high-dimensional space.

::: {.col-left style="margin-top: 0.6em;"}
**What "good beam" means at the nozzle:**

- Spot size σ within spec (e.g. ≤ 5 mm at isocentre)
- Energy spread < 1%
- Position within ± 1 mm
:::

::: {.col-right style="margin-top: 0.6em;"}
::: {.highlight-box}
**Bayesian Optimisation is a natural fit:**

- Works in 2–20 dimensions
- Sample-efficient: ~50 evaluations vs. thousands for grid search
- Model-free: works on the real machine

Deployed at AWAKE (CERN), FLASH (DESY), and clinical proton therapy centres.
:::
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
Sample efficiency is the key point. Each beam measurement takes ~30 seconds on a clinical machine. You want an algorithm that finds a good solution in as few evaluations as possible. BO is designed for exactly this regime: expensive-to-evaluate, black-box objectives.
:::

---

## Cheetah — Differentiable Beam Physics in PyTorch

::: {.col-left}
**What Cheetah is:**

- PyTorch-based beam dynamics simulation
- Drifts, quads, dipoles, RF cavities, screens
- **Differentiable** → gradients flow through the simulation
- Milliseconds per evaluation · `pip install cheetah-accelerator`

**Why it matters here:**

- We use Cheetah as the "virtual machine" in the notebooks
- Same code structure you'd use with a real machine
:::

::: {.col-right}

```{python}
import torch, cheetah

segment = cheetah.Segment(elements=[
    cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(0.5)),
    cheetah.Quadrupole(length=torch.tensor(0.1), name="QF"),
    cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(1.0)),
    cheetah.Quadrupole(length=torch.tensor(0.1), name="QD"),
    cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(0.5)),
    cheetah.Screen(name="monitor"),
])

# 150 MeV proton beam
beam_in = cheetah.ParameterBeam.from_twiss(
    energy=torch.tensor(1088.3e6),  # total energy in eV
    beta_x=torch.tensor(1.0),
    beta_y=torch.tensor(1.0),
    emittance_x=torch.tensor(1e-6),
    emittance_y=torch.tensor(1e-6),
    species=cheetah.Species("proton"),
)

beam_out = segment.track(beam_in)
print(f"σ_x = {beam_out.sigma_x.item()*1e3:.2f} mm")
```

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
Cheetah was developed at DESY for the AWAKE experiment and the European XFEL. The key feature: because it is a PyTorch module, gradients flow through the beam tracking. This enables gradient descent directly on machine parameters — without ever touching the real machine.

The code structure for a Cheetah optimisation loop is identical to what you'd write for a real machine — you just replace `segment.track(beam_in)` with a call to your machine's measurement interface.
:::

---

## Bayesian Optimisation: Finding Focus in 40 Evaluations

```{python}
from skopt import gp_minimize
from skopt.space import Real

def objective(params):
    k1_qf, k1_qd = params
    segment.QF.k1 = torch.tensor(k1_qf, dtype=torch.float32)
    segment.QD.k1 = torch.tensor(k1_qd, dtype=torch.float32)
    beam_out = segment.track(beam_in)
    result = (beam_out.sigma_x + beam_out.sigma_y).item()
    return result if np.isfinite(result) else 1.0  # m

result = gp_minimize(
    func=objective,
    dimensions=[Real(-10.0, 10.0, name="k1_QF"),
                Real(-10.0, 10.0, name="k1_QD")],
    n_calls=40,          # 40 beam measurements
    n_initial_points=8,  # random exploration before GP kicks in
    random_state=42,
)
# → best σ_x + σ_y = 4.36 mm  (vs 4.83 mm for k₁ = 0)
```

::: {.col-left}
::: {.metric}
BO finds **4.36 mm**
Random search: **4.41 mm**
No quads: **4.83 mm**
:::
:::

::: {.col-right}
::: {.qr-box}
**Notebook 02** — includes convergence plot and gradient descent comparison
:::
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
Results from running the actual notebook locally. The GP surrogate inside BO finds a better solution than random search with the same evaluation budget.

The gradient descent comparison is an interesting bonus: starting at k₁=0, the gradient of (σ_x + σ_y) with respect to each k₁ is nearly zero — because focusing in x defocuses in y by almost the same amount. BO has no such issue because it doesn't rely on gradients.

This is a genuine insight: sometimes the objective landscape is flat in the gradient direction, and derivative-free methods are more robust.
:::

# Use Case 3 {.section-divider background-color="#0a1520"}

::: {style="color: #22d3ee; font-size: 1.6em; font-weight: 800; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
Surrogate Models
:::

Replacing tracking codes with neural networks

---

## The Speed Problem

**Tracking codes are slow:**

| Code | Typical runtime |
|---|---|
| TraceWin (RFQ / LINAC) | 1–10 min per evaluation |
| G4beamline (Geant4 transport) | 10–60 min |
| FLUKA (dosimetry) | Hours |
| Cheetah (our "fast" simulator) | ~0.4 ms |

For real-time control or online BO, you need millisecond response — not minutes.

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.8em;"}
**The solution:** train a neural network on simulation outputs once.
Call the NN instead of the simulator during optimisation.
Typical speedup: **10³ – 10⁵×** · typical error: **< 1%** in the training domain.
:::

::: notes
This is the most widely deployed AI technique in accelerator physics today. Surrogates are used at CERN for FCC design studies, at JLab for CEBAF operations, and in proton therapy for dose calculation acceleration.

The key workflow: (1) run the slow code offline for thousands of random parameter settings; (2) train a neural network on these input-output pairs; (3) call the NN during optimisation instead of the slow code.
:::

---

## Training the Surrogate

```{python}
import numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset

# Step 1: generate 5000 Cheetah evaluations as training data
def run_cheetah(k1_qf, k1_qd):
    segment.QF.k1 = torch.tensor(k1_qf, dtype=torch.float32)
    segment.QD.k1 = torch.tensor(k1_qd, dtype=torch.float32)
    b = segment.track(beam_in)
    return [b.sigma_x.item() * 1e3, b.sigma_y.item() * 1e3]  # mm

# Step 2: MLP with Tanh activations (smooth physics → smooth surrogate)
class BeamSurrogate(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(2, 128), nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(128, 2),         # predict (σ_x, σ_y)
        )
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)
```

::: notes
Tanh activations: for a surrogate of smooth physics, Tanh often outperforms ReLU because it produces smoother interpolations between training points.

We only predict σ_x and σ_y — the centroids μ_x and μ_y are always 0 for our symmetric on-axis beam, so they carry no information.

Training on 5000 Cheetah evaluations takes ~3 seconds with the parallel batch infrastructure.
:::

## Results: Accuracy and Speed

::: {.col-left}

**Accuracy on 1000 held-out test points:**

| Output | R² | MAE |
|---|---|---|
| σ_x | **1.0000** | 0.0006 mm |
| σ_y | **1.0000** | 0.0006 mm |

**Speed (1000 evaluations):**

| Method | Time |
|---|---|
| Cheetah (serial) | 371 ms |
| Surrogate (batched) | **0.6 ms** |
| **Speedup** | **586×** |

:::

::: {.col-right}

**BO with surrogate as oracle:**

```{python}
# Replace Cheetah with surrogate in the BO loop
def objective_surrogate(params):
    x = torch.tensor(params, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(0)
    with torch.no_grad():
        y = denormalise(surrogate(normalise(x)))
    return (y[0, 0] + y[0, 1]).item() * 1e-3
```

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.6em;"}
BO-surrogate finds **4.36 mm** — identical to BO-Cheetah.
Ground-truth Cheetah validation: **4.36 mm** ✓
:::

:::

:::

::: {.qr-box}
**Notebook 03** — timing benchmark · parity plot · ensemble UQ
:::

::: notes
These numbers are from running the actual notebook. R²=1.0000 means the surrogate is essentially perfect for this simple 2-parameter lattice.

The surrogate-in-the-loop result is the key proof: BO finds the same optimum whether it uses Cheetah or the trained surrogate. The surrogate is a faithful oracle for this problem.

For more complex problems (TraceWin, G4beamline), the surrogate approximation error matters more, but the speedup justification becomes even stronger.
:::

## From Surrogate to Digital Twin

::: {.col-left}

A **surrogate** answers:
*"What does the simulation predict for these settings?"*

A **digital twin** answers:
*"What is my actual machine doing right now?"*

::: {.highlight-box style="margin-top: 0.6em;"}
**The difference:**

Surrogate = fast offline model

Digital twin = surrogate + live sensor data + continuous update loop
:::

:::

::: {.col-right}

**Medical accelerator use cases:**

- **Virtual commissioning** — test control strategies before beam-on
- **Adaptive QA** — twin detects drift, flags recalibration
- **Fault simulation** — inject virtual faults to train operators
- **Cross-facility transfer** — twin from one centre adapted to another

::: {.key-result .fragment style="margin-top: 0.6em;"}
**TwinRISE** (Horizon Europe, 2026–2030): federated digital twins for accelerators across 19 institutions in 7 countries.
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
TwinRISE is the Horizon project I'm coordinating at GANIL. The key innovation: federated learning means each facility trains locally and shares only model updates (not raw data), preserving data sovereignty — important for clinical sites.

The "cross-facility learning" point is crucial for medical machines: if a model can be pre-trained on a well-instrumented research machine and then fine-tuned on a clinical machine with limited data, we solve the data scarcity problem that defines clinical AI.
:::

---

## Open Problems — What AI Cannot Yet Solve

::: {.col-left}

**1. Data scarcity on clinical machines**

Fault data is rare by design. Transfer learning from research machines is promising but not solved. Physics-informed models can regularise with little data.

**2. Explainability for regulatory compliance**

IEC 62304 and EU AI Act (high-risk classification) require auditable, interpretable decisions. "Why did the model flag this pulse?" must have an answer.

**3. Cross-facility transfer**

A model trained at Centre A rarely works at Centre B without retraining. Federated learning + domain adaptation are the frontier.

:::

::: {.col-right}

**4. Real-time deployment**

Clinical LINACs run proprietary interfaces (Varian, Elekta, IBA). Deploying a PyTorch model inside a real-time control system is an engineering challenge as much as a scientific one.

**5. Foundation models for accelerators**

No pre-trained accelerator model exists yet (analogous to LLMs for text). Would require pooled data across facilities — a governance challenge. ARTIFACT / TwinRISE are building the infrastructure.

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.8em;"}
These are open research problems — not blockers. AI is already deployed and delivering value in clinical accelerator operations today.
:::

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
I want to be honest about what isn't solved. This is a school lecture, not a marketing presentation.

The EU AI Act (2024) classifies AI in safety-critical control systems as "high-risk," requiring conformity assessment, human oversight, and documentation. This raises the bar significantly compared to research use.

The foundation model question is the 5-year horizon. AlphaFold-style pre-training on pooled waveform data from all superconducting accelerators in Europe could give any facility a strong starting model. That's the vision TwinRISE is building toward.
:::

## Summary

::: {.col-left}

::: {.key-result}
**1. Physics invented ML**

Hopfield networks and Boltzmann machines trace directly to condensed matter and statistical mechanics. The 2024 Nobel in Physics is a formal recognition. We are natural practitioners.
:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.6em;"}
**2. The medical context inverts the ML problem**

Clinical constraints (safety, uptime, regulation) mean scarce data and strict explainability requirements. Design for scarcity: autoencoders, BO, physics-informed models.
:::

:::

::: {.col-right}

::: {.key-result}

Three takeaways — then Q&A. Common questions to anticipate:

"What accuracy do you need for the surrogate to be clinically useful?" → depends on application. For pre-treatment QA, sub-percent. For real-time corrections, tighter.

"Is any of this approved as medical device software?" → not yet at the AI decision level. Current deployment is as decision-support (physicist confirms), not autonomous control.
